name: Esther Ibrahim

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Thanks for making time. I work for the Work Futures Panel, an independent research group with no ties to AI companies, employers, unions, parties or government. Everything you say stays confidential, so you can tell me what you would say in public and, separately, what you really think. To start, can you walk me through a normal working day?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: There isn't really a normal day, which is half the point. Lunch and dinner I'm on the e-bike doing takeaway in the city centre, on three apps at once. In the afternoon gap I switch to the car and do same-day parcels for a fourth app. I've got an AI assistant on my phone that tells me which app is paying best per hour right now, and it's usually right.

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: What do you like about it, and what wears you out?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I like that I can game it. Most riders take whatever pings first; I check the rate per kilometre and turn down the bad ones, so I earn more than most. What wears me out is rain, and restaurants that keep you waiting twenty minutes for one burger. My partner Sami is a bus mechanic, so at least one of us has normal hours.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The first picture is called AI Plateau. "Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway." If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say I told you so, to be honest, because people at the restaurant counters keep saying the robots are coming next year. Online I'd post a little rant about all the money that went into hype. Then I'd go back to work.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: For me it's nearly perfect. If AI stays dumb, I stay the smartest thing on the delivery map, and the three apps keep fighting over me on a Friday night. My pay stays high because I'm good at picking jobs. The only thing that worries me is the apps cutting rates, and that happens with or without AI.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Keep doing what I'm doing, basically. I'd keep putting 500 a month into my index fund and keep the nine months of savings topped up. I'd probably try the new versions of the AI tools anyway, because I like them. Maybe I'd look at a cargo e-bike, which costs about 4,000 but lets me take bigger orders.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calm, a bit smug maybe. It's a world I already know how to win in.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What's the thing that actually threatens your income in that world?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Pay cuts. Last spring one of the apps cut the base fee by a fifth overnight, no warning. That's why I'm on four apps and not one. If one drops me, the others don't.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said it's nearly perfect. Is it?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: It's not perfect, no. My knees and my lungs in winter aren't going to love this forever. I'd give it five more years on the bike, then maybe move to just the car.

say: I'd say **I told you so** to the people predicting robots next year.
Online I'd **rant** about all the money spent on hype.
think: A dumb AI keeps her the **smartest player** on the delivery apps.
The real threat is **rate cuts** by the apps, which happen regardless of AI.
do: Keep putting **500 a month** into her index fund and keep savings topped up.
Keep using **AI tools** to choose the best-paying orders.
Price a **cargo e-bike** at about 4,000 to take bigger orders.
feel: She feels **calm** and a little smug about a world she knows how to win in.
S0.quote: If AI stays dumb, I stay the smartest thing on the delivery map, and the three apps keep fighting over me on a Friday night.
fieldNote: She sees **multi-apping** as her protection: no single app can sink her income.
She is already planning her own exit from the **bike** in about five years.
Strong savings and an **index fund** mean she can absorb a sudden rate cut.

steps.text: Keep riding lunch and dinner shifts across three food apps
Put 500 a month into the index fund
Price a 4,000 cargo e-bike for bigger orders

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The second picture is called Steady Disruption. "Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many thinking tasks in many jobs: writing, checking, planning, buying, booking, coding and answering customers. Robots spread into hands-on work more slowly. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. Most people still have work, and there is some time to adjust." If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say it's good for us riders, at least for a while, because the stuff AI does is the office stuff. Online I'd tell people to start using the tools now. At the restaurant counter I'd say the same thing to the other riders, who'd roll their eyes at me.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Every app on my phone gets cleverer in this picture, and so do I. The bike still needs legs, and mine are paid by the hour. The risk is that the apps use AI to squeeze us, with perfect pricing so nobody can pick the good jobs anymore. My edge is picking jobs, so that worries me a bit.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd try every new AI tool in the first month and keep the ones that actually raise my hourly rate. I'd start a short online course in logistics planning, the free one I saw from the city college, about three months long. I'd also keep an eye on the robot delivery pilot in the north of the city and see who they're hiring. I'd keep about 10,000 in savings untouched.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Pretty calm, actually. Interested more than worried. It's like a new app launching: there's money in being early.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would make you change your mind and worry?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: If the apps price every job perfectly, the trick I use stops working. Then I'm earning what everyone else earns, which is less. I'd probably notice it in my weekly totals within a month, and I'd look harder at the planning course then.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What's the robot pilot you mentioned?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The sidewalk robots, the little six-wheeled boxes. They're slow and they get stuck on kerbs. But the people who watch them from a screen get paid more than riders, I checked.

say: This round is **good for riders** at first, because AI takes the office tasks.
I'd tell people online to start using the **tools now**.
think: AI could let apps price jobs so well that her **job-picking edge** disappears.
Hands-on delivery still needs **legs**, so her hourly work stays for now.
do: Test every new **AI tool** in the first month and keep the profitable ones.
Take a free three-month **logistics planning** course at the city college.
Watch the **robot delivery pilot** in the north of the city and see who it hires.
feel: She feels **calm** and curious, like an early user of a new app.
S1.quote: Every app on my phone gets cleverer in this picture, and so do I. The bike still needs legs, and mine are paid by the hour.
fieldNote: Her one fear is **perfect pricing** removing her advantage over other riders.
She has already checked the **pay of robot supervisors**, which shows how early she moves.
She keeps **10,000** untouched as a safety net.

steps.text: Test new AI tools and keep those that raise her hourly rate
Take the city college's free logistics planning course
Check who the sidewalk robot pilot is hiring

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The third picture is called AGI by 2028. "Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2031. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare." If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say get ready, loudly, to anyone who'd listen. I'd post about which skills I'm learning and what robot companies are paying. Riders would call me a traitor for a week and then ask me how I did it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Off the record, it's scary for my job, full stop. Robots doing my job by 2031 means I need to be the person watching ten robots from a screen by 2030, not the person they replace. Thinking AI coming first doesn't hurt me much, because my job is legs and roads. But it means the robot companies get very smart very fast.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd apply to the robot delivery pilot straight away, for any job, even weekend shifts, just to get inside. I'd do a robotics maintenance certificate in the evenings, about a year. I'd keep riding to pay for it and cut the index fund to 200 a month so I'd have more cash on hand. I'd also talk to Sami about whether his bus depot will need people for electric fleets, because that might be a second door.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious. Not panicked, I've got savings and I'm fast on my feet. But two years to the AI and five to the robots is tight for someone with only school qualifications.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What could stop you getting one of those jobs?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Every rider wants the same robot jobs, and there aren't many. One person watching ten robots means nine riders out. That's the bit that keeps me honest: I could easily be one of the nine.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You sound confident but you've called it scary. Which is it?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: What makes me anxious is the timing, not the end. I think I'll be fine in 2035. It's 2031 and 2032 that look rough, the gap between the robots arriving and me having the right job.

say: I'd tell everyone to **get ready**, and share which skills pay.
Riders would call me a **traitor** for a week, then ask how I did it.
think: Robots by 2031 mean she must **supervise robots** by 2030 or be replaced.
One supervisor per ten robots means **nine riders out**, possibly including her.
do: Apply to the **robot delivery pilot** for any job, even weekends.
Study for a **robotics maintenance** certificate in the evenings for a year.
Cut the index fund to **200 a month** to hold more cash.
feel: She feels **anxious** about the gap years of 2031 and 2032.
She still trusts her **speed** and savings to carry her through.
S2.quote: Robots doing my job by 2031 means I need to be the person watching ten robots from a screen by 2030, not the person they replace.
fieldNote: She separates **the end point**, which she trusts, from the gap years, which scare her.
She openly counts herself among the **nine riders** who might lose out.
Her partner's **bus depot** is a second route she would explore.

steps.text: Apply for any role at the sidewalk robot delivery pilot
Study a one-year robotics maintenance certificate in the evenings
Cut index fund payments to 200 a month to hold cash
Ask Sami's bus depot about electric fleet jobs

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The fourth picture is called AGI by 2031. "Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2034. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast." If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say we've got a window and riders should use it. At the counters I'd point people to the courses. Online I'd probably start a small channel about getting out of riding, half for fun.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I think this is about the right speed for me. Eight years until the robots is enough to get a robotics certificate and be the one fixing the sidewalk robots that replace couriers like me. The thinking AI in 2031 mostly changes the apps, and I'm good with apps.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd keep riding for the next three years and keep the index fund at 500 a month. I'd start the robotics certificate in 2028, once I know which robot company is winning in the city. I'd apply for supervisor jobs around 2031. With the extra cash I might even buy a share in a small charging hub with a friend, because robots need charging too.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: A little uneasy, mostly because things rarely run on schedule. But it feels like I'd have time to do it properly.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What if the robot companies are late?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Then I'd have a certificate and nowhere to use it, which would be annoying. But the course would still teach me electrics and fixing things. I'd rather have the skill early than late.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you give up to fit in the course?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Riding, mostly, and some sleep. I'm not giving up the bike money until I have to. Sami says I treat my life like a delivery route, always looking for the faster turn.

say: Riders have a **window** and should use it.
I might start a small **online channel** about leaving riding.
think: Eight years is enough to become the one **fixing sidewalk robots**.
Thinking AI in 2031 mostly changes the **apps**, which she handles well.
do: Keep riding and investing **500 a month** for the next three years.
Start the **robotics certificate** in 2028 once a winning company is clear.
Consider a **charging hub** share with a friend.
feel: She feels **slightly uneasy**, mainly that schedules slip.
She feels she would have **time** to do it properly.
S3.quote: Eight years until the robots is enough to get a robotics certificate and be the one fixing the sidewalk robots that replace couriers like me.
fieldNote: She times training to **which company wins**, a very market-minded choice.
The **charging hub** idea shows her instinct to own a piece of the new system.
Her partner describes her as always seeking the **faster turn**.

steps.text: Keep riding three food apps for three more years
Buy a share in a robot charging hub with a friend
Apply for robot supervisor jobs around 2031

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The last picture is called AGI by 2036. "Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2039. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans." If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say ten years is a whole career for a delivery rider. Nobody I know has done this job for ten years anyway. Online I'd say it's a good time to be young and flexible.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Honestly I think it's fine for me. I'll be 37 when the robots arrive, and I'd planned to be off the bike long before. The AI years before that would probably give me better tools to run something of my own.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd ride for another four or five years and keep investing. Around 2030 I'd move into dispatching or fleet work, maybe run a small group of riders for a restaurant chain. I'd use AI for all the scheduling so I can manage more people. By 2036 I'd want to be on the side that buys the robots, not the side that gets replaced.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calm, mostly. It feels like a long runway, and I like a long runway.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What about the riders who've been doing it longer?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Some of them are already gone, to be fair. Riders come and go in a year or two. For the older ones who've done it for fifteen years, ten years is harder, because they'd be in their fifties and starting again.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you use the extra time for, outside work?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Maybe a small family, around 32 or 33. With ten years I wouldn't have to choose between that and changing jobs. I'd do the change first and then the baby, probably.

say: Ten years is a **whole career** for a delivery rider.
It's a good time to be **young and flexible**.
think: At 37 she planned to be **off the bike** anyway.
AI tools could help her **run something** of her own first.
do: Ride for **four or five years** more while investing.
Move into **dispatch or fleet work** around 2030, using AI for scheduling.
Aim to be a **robot buyer** by 2036, not replaced by one.
feel: She feels **calm** with a long runway ahead.
S4.quote: Ten years is a whole career for a delivery rider. Nobody I know has done this job for ten years anyway.
fieldNote: For a **young rider**, ten years is longer than most careers in the job.
She worries more for **older riders** in their fifties than for herself.
She would fit a **family** around the switch, career change first.

steps.text: Keep riding and investing for four or five years
Move into dispatch or fleet management around 2030
Use AI scheduling tools to manage a rider team
Plan a baby after the career switch, around 33

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: AGI by 2028, because of the gap years when the robots are here and I'm not ready. What would help is if the robot companies had to train the riders they replace, a real certificate paid for by them. I've never been loyal to an app, so I'm not going to start being loyal to a job that's leaving.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: Ask about the restaurants. They hate the apps' fees more than we do. If robots are cheaper, they'll switch in a heartbeat, and that's when it really moves.

headlineQuote: I've never been loyal to an app, so I'm not going to start being loyal to a job that's leaving.
portrait: Esther is a **27-year-old** rider who works four delivery apps and uses AI daily to pick the best jobs.
She lives with **Sami**, a bus mechanic, and has nine months saved plus an **index fund**.
She is **adaptive** and market-minded, always looking for the faster turn.
She stays calm in slow pictures and grows **anxious** only in AGI by 2028, about the gap years.
Her plan is to move from riding into **robot supervision** or fleet work before robots arrive.
biggestWorry: AGI by 2028, because of the **gap years** when robots arrive before she has the right job.
whatWouldHelp: Robot companies paying to **train the riders** they replace, with a real certificate.
